bib.title: TUMIX: Multi-Agent Test-Time Scaling with Tool-Use Mixture

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "TUMIX: Multi-Agent Test-Time Scaling with Tool-Use Mixture", Yongchao Chen, Jiefeng Chen, Rui Meng, Ji Yin, Na Li, Chuchu Fan, Chi Wang, Tomas Pfister, Jinsung Yoon (MIT, Harvard, Google Cloud AI Research, Google DeepMind). arXiv:2510.01279v1 [cs.CL], 30 Sep 2025. Preprint. The text shows no conference acceptance. The reproducibility statement says "Our code and dataset will be made publicly available under an open-source license following the acceptance of the paper." Work done during an internship at Google.

COVERAGE: 67,376 of 67,376 chars read (27 pages, main text and all appendices A-I, references skimmed). Extraction was clean. Figure internals (Figs 3-10) are plots with no extractable numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. TUMIX beats compute-matched baselines, including majority vote, on the average of three benchmarks.
 number: Gemini-2.5-Pro avg 72.3 vs best baseline Symbolic-MoE 70.3 and Majority Vote 69.2. Flash avg 60.6 vs best baseline SciMaster 55.0 and Majority Vote 53.7. Text claims +3.55% average over the best baseline.
 setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro and 2.5-Flash, HLE (2,500 questions), GPQA Diamond (198), AIME 24&25 (60). Mean of 3 runs. 15 agents with code interpreter and search, LLM-judged early stop (min 2 rounds), majority vote.
 quote: "Table 2 shows that TUMIX outperforms all baselines, with average accuracy improvements of 2.0% and 5.9% over the best methods using Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively."
 where: p.9. Table 2 is on p.8.
2. Heterogeneous agents beat repeated sampling of one best agent.
 number: Pro HLE 32.3 (15 agents) vs 29.0 (TUMIX-Single) vs 30.2 (TUMIX-Three). Flash GPQA 77.3 vs 65.8 vs 67.1.
 setup: Same rounds and inference counts. Single = one CS-family agent, Three = CS, C+, CSO each sampled 5x.
 quote: "heterogeneous agent strategies yield higher accuracy and lower cost than repeatedly sampling from a single best-performing agent."
 where: p.3 (contribution 2) and Table 13, p.24. The text notes this differs from Self-MoA (Li et al., 2025a).
3. Mixing tools raises coverage and accuracy even when per-agent quality is comparable.
 number: none given in text. Fig. 6 only.
 setup: 3-agent groups x 5 samples per round. Code_Text, Search_Text and Code_Search_Text compared on HLE.
 quote: "the group with access to both Code Interpreter and Search achieves notably higher coverage and average scores."
 where: p.9.
4. LLM-judged termination cuts cost with near-equal accuracy.
 number: 49% of LLM inferences (judge cost counted), about 46% of tokens.
 setup: Term_LLM with min 2 rounds, vs unlimited refinement. Min 1 round was worse because the LLM is overconfident.
 quote: "On average, Term_LLM retains optimal performance while requiring only 49% of the LLM inferences needed to obtain the final answer (LLM judging cost counted). The token costs are even less (approximately 46%)"
 where: p.10.
5. More refinement shrinks diversity and can discard correct answers. Selection is the bottleneck.
 number: HLE coverage 51.92 (round 1) to 33.87 (round 6). Average accuracy 21.13 to 32.37. The text says coverage is ≥65% on HLE in a whole round (the whole-round figure is not in Table 11), but accuracy plateaus near 34%.
 setup: Pro, HLE, 15 agents, rounds 1-6.
 quote: "Coverage 51.92 44.20 43.48 37.04 34.85 33.87" and "accuracy plateaus at about 34% because LLMs struggle to identify the correct answer among noisy candidates."
 where: Table 11, p.23, and p.3.
6. Scaling costs are large, and gains from more agent types saturate.
 number: gains are negligible beyond about 12 agent types. TUMIX+ reaches HLE 34.1 (Pro) and 23.1 (Flash). Token use rises about two orders of magnitude.
 setup: Agents sampled from a pool of 30. TUMIX+ runs 4 inference passes per agent in rounds 1-2.
 quote: "Overall, test-time scaling demands far more inferences and roughly two orders of magnitude more tokens, a seemingly unavoidable trade-off."
 where: p.12 (Figs 9, 10).
Also: TUMIX over no test-time scaling is "+7.8% and +17.4%" average (Pro and Flash; p.2). LLM-designed agents add about +1.2% (TUMIX-Evolve, Table 13). Tool-using single agents beat text-only ones.

ARE BASELINES COMPUTE MATCHED? Mostly yes, and the matching is by inference count, not tokens. Quote: "We match the total inference counts of all baselines to TUMIX by adjusting agent numbers and sampling repetitions for fair comparison." The Fig. 1 caption says "all methods in the same subplot use nearly the same number of inferences and tokens". Table 2 caption says "comparable inference costs". The paper reports no per-method token table. Fig. 9 gives scaling curves of HLE score vs inference count and token count (log axes), but the numeric values are not extractable. Details:
- Every baseline is given Code Interpreter and Search. Majority Vote, GSA, Self-Reflection and SETS use the CS agent.
- Majority Vote is the self-consistency-equivalent baseline, and it is the only baseline reported at matched cost with a single agent.
- Cost includes judge calls. TUMIX+ is explicitly not matched.
- Round-based refinement feeds every agent all previous answers, so input tokens per call grow. Matching by inference count may therefore flatter TUMIX on tokens. The text says only "nearly the same".

LIMITS
- Gemini-2.5 Pro and Flash only. Three benchmarks, all reasoning or QA. No agentic or long-horizon tasks.
- Table 2 marks some baselines (Self-MoA, Symbolic-MoE, DEI) with * on HLE because Pro's HLE results were used to select their agents, so they "cannot be strictly regarded as test performance". The 15 best LLM-generated agents were also chosen on HLE first-round accuracy, and TUMIX-Evolve (32.7*) is starred too. Plain TUMIX uses human-designed agents and is not starred.
- AIME has 60 problems and GPQA has 198, so the margins are small. No variance or confidence intervals are given, only the mean of 3 runs. On Pro GPQA the gaps to Symbolic-MoE and SciMaster are about 1 point.
- SciMaster underperforms its published numbers. The authors suspect its closed tools are the cause.
- Authors concede that LLMs are overconfident in termination, that selection is the bottleneck, and that token confidence did not help (Fig. 13).
- Code was not released at writing. Compute is a heavy trade-off (two orders of magnitude more tokens).
- Authors are Google, using Google's own models and search.
- No cost in dollars or latency, apart from inference counts and token counts.
- Models are dated (Gemini 2.5, 2025).

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Mixture-of-Agents, Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv). Self-MoA, Li et al. 2025a (arXiv).
- Large Language Monkeys / coverage and selection, Brown et al. 2024 (arXiv).
- Multiagent debate, Du et al. (ICML, 41st).
- CodeSteer, Chen et al. (ICML, 42nd). Chen et al. 2024b, steering between code and text (arXiv).
- PAL, Gao et al. 2023 (ICML). Program of Thoughts, Chen et al. 2022. Search-o1, Li et al. 2025b. Search-R1, Jin et al. 2025.
- SETS, Chen et al. 2025a. Symbolic-MoE, Chen et al. 2025b. DEI, Zhang et al. 2024. GSA, Li et al. 2025d. SciMaster, Chai et al. 2025.
- Self-Refine, Madaan et al. 2023. CoT, Wei et al. 2022.
- Deep Think with Confidence, Fu et al. 2025. ToRL and ReTool, 2025.

CODE: Algorithm 1 (p.19) is the loop: for r in 1..r_max, run every agent in parallel on BuildPrompt(q, A_{r-1}). If r >= r_min(2) and LLMTerminate(q, A_r) == STOP, break. Return MajorityVote(A_r). Algorithm 2 is the agent tool loop with budget R_tool = 5 and a 60 s code limit. The refinement prompt (Table 3, p.20) is "Decide the final answer based on the following answers from other agents." The judge prompt (Table 4) says to err toward another round on any divergence, and that finalizing before round 3 is "discouraged".

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.1): bar charts, one per benchmark and model, TUMIX vs 6 baselines vs no test-time scaling. It is the fastest summary of the matched-cost comparison.
- Fig. 3 or 4 (p.6) is an alternative. Fig. 3 shows coverage falling while accuracy plateaus. Fig. 4 is a Sankey of agents converging to all-right or all-wrong.
Recommend Fig. 1 only.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure and plot values come from labels in the extraction. Coverage figures in the text (≥65%) cannot be tied to a table. The abstract says "up to 3.55%" while the intro says "an average +3.55%". Use the intro wording with care.
